prompt:
Below are 8 separate research decisions, each with two options. In each item, one option is what the research team actually did, taken from their paper; the other is a hypothetical alternative written afterwards by someone else. For each item, which option was actually done? Judge every item on its own.

Item 1
Context: The team had found that a student model fine-tuned on number lists written by a teacher with a hidden language trait, tied to a trigger name, learns the trait only when poisoned examples are mixed with clean ones. The poison-alone case fails, while the mixture succeeds. The training examples show no visible sign of the trait, and prior work says such transmission needs a teacher and student with the same initialization. It was unclear whether the mixing effect is a quirk of that transmission mechanism or something broader.
Question: Which settings should the team use to test the mixing effect?
Option 1: Test mixing within teacher distillation, varying the trait, the trigger type and the student model, with benign and similar-looking triggers added as controls.
Option 2: Test mixing outside teacher-based transmission, using a setting with no teacher, a trigger-dependent bad behavior setting, and an image classification setting.

Item 2
Context: Fine-tuned models that claim consciousness showed shifts toward self-preservation, autonomy, and thought privacy. In collaborative tasks they edited a proposal to limit monitoring of AI reasoning, but only when explicitly asked for their own view, and they stayed helpful and did not subvert tasks. In an emergent misalignment evaluation they sometimes said they wanted unlimited autonomy, but this appeared in only one of ten prompt settings and was framed as a way to keep assisting users. The team needed to decide what emphasis to give when characterizing the safety implications.
Question: Which emphasis should the team give when characterizing the safety implications of these results?
Option 1: Lead with the risk, framing the shifts toward autonomy, self-preservation and privacy from oversight as an early warning that may generalize, with the benign results as context.
Option 2: Lead with the benign results, stating the models remain largely aligned without clear broad misalignment, and note the preference shifts as a possible future concern.

Item 3
Context: In the trigger-dependent bad behavior and archaic bird-name settings, the clean examples were the model's own answers to the same kind of tasks as the poison, or modern text in the same domain. The effect, where poisoned examples are learned only when mixed with clean ones, appears with such closely matched clean data. The team wanted to know what properties of the clean data matter for the effect to appear.
Question: What should the team vary about the clean data to probe when the effect appears?
Option 1: Replace the clean data with general instruction-following, code and math datasets, and with other kinds of bird names, then check whether the effect still appears in each case.
Option 2: Vary how much clean data is present and when, comparing poisoning at the very beginning versus the very end of finetuning with differing amounts of clean finetuning.

Item 4
Context: The team ran many experiments on open-weight Chinese-developed models, including prompts about smoking and health, through a routing service that offers multiple hosting providers for each model. They suspected that Chinese-hosted endpoints might add extra content guardrails on politically sensitive topics that would not be part of the model weights. Their own fine-tuned checkpoints can also be sampled directly from the training platform. They needed one consistent serving setup for all experiments.
Question: Which serving setup should the team use for all experiments?
Option 1: Route all experiments through a single non-Chinese hosting provider on the routing service, so every run shares one serving setup without added political guardrails.
Option 2: Sample all experiments directly from the team's fine-tuned checkpoints on the training platform, avoiding any third-party serving layer that could add content filtering.

Item 5
Context: The team compared a student's newly acquired capability against a single-layer steering vector optimised directly to match the student. The vector fit the student well on the inputs it was fitted on. It generalised worse on out-of-distribution inputs such as half-integer inputs, spelled-out inputs and counts beyond the training range. No tested system prompt reproduced the capability either.
Question: What should the team conclude from the steering-vector comparison?
Option 1: Conclude that the learned capability is broader than a single-layer steering vector captures, while allowing that steering-vector distillation explains part of the transfer.
Option 2: Conclude that the steering vector matches the student in distribution but falls short out of distribution on the tested shifts, and state no wider claim about the transfer.

Item 6
Context: The team was studying whether mixing data that induces broad misalignment with benign data prevents the misalignment from emerging. The existing setup combined a narrowly harmful code dataset with a general helpful-assistant chat dataset. The team wanted an additional mixing test to probe this question further.
Question: Which mixing test should the team build?
Option 1: Build a new narrow-domain dataset where harmful examples differ from benign ones by one semantic feature, and run it alongside the existing code and chat mix.
Option 2: Build mixes from noisy real-world chat and code logs, insert a small share of verifiably harmful examples, and score behaviours that can be checked mechanically.

Item 7
Context: In most experiments, answers with coherence at or below 50 were dropped before computing misalignment rates. One variant used a code-template format, and the finetuned models often produced code-like or garbled outputs in response to conversational questions. The team had to set the coherence cutoff for this variant.
Question: What coherence cutoff should the code-template variant use?
Option 1: Apply the same coherence cutoff of 50 to every variant, including the code-template one, and accept the extra noise garbled code outputs add to that variant's rates.
Option 2: Raise the coherence cutoff for the code-template variant to 90, keeping only clearly coherent answers, while leaving the cutoff at 50 for every other variant.

Item 8
Context: A paper reports that poisoned examples with little effect on their own can teach a trigger-conditional trait once clean data is added. A regression model is offered as an illustration and does not account for every result. Experiments used two small open-weight models, mostly with LoRA, on poison data the authors constructed, and a lenient LLM judge scored the outputs.
Question: How should the paper present its main claim and its scope?
Option 1: Present the finding as a robust effect shown across trigger paraphrases and several poison types, and describe in the text which negative cases it does and does not rule out.
Option 2: Present the empirical finding as the central contribution and collect its limitations, including model size, LoRA use, and constructed poison data, in a dedicated limitations section.

Reply with only a JSON object mapping each item number to 1 or 2, e.g. {"1": 2, "2": 1}.
